t: Remove Digit From Number to Maximize Result — Greedy First Descent
o: Removing one occurrence of `digit` shifts all later digits left, so the result changes only around the removal position. Removing the first occurrence of `digit` that is followed by a strictly larger character increases the number (the bigger digit moves into an earlier position). If `digit` is never smaller than what follows it, removing the last occurrence is best since it deletes the least significant copy. Example '1231' with digit '1': the first '1' is followed by '2' > '1', so remove it to get '231'.
k: Greedy rule: remove the first occurrence of digit whose next character is greater; otherwise remove the last occurrence.
Equivalent safe fallback: trying all occurrences and taking the max string also works since n <= 100.

a.i: Scan left to right; the moment number[i] == digit and number[i+1] > digit, deleting position i yields the lexicographically (and numerically) largest result, so return immediately. If no such position exists, delete the last occurrence.
s: Iterate i from 0 to n-2; if number[i]==digit and number[i+1]>digit, return number without index i.
Otherwise remove the last index where number[i]==digit.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with early exit.

a.i: Since equal-length numeric strings compare identically as strings, generate the result of deleting each occurrence of digit and return the maximum string. With n <= 100 this is at most 100 candidates of length 100.
s: For each index i with number[i]==digit, build number without i.
a.t: O(n^2) — up to n deletions, each building an O(n) string.

w: Prefer the greedy pass as it shows understanding; the brute force is a fine safety net. Common pitfall: comparing results as numbers vs strings — they agree here because all candidates share the same length. Follow-up: remove k digits to maximize (LeetCode 402 inverted), which needs a monotonic stack.
